articles.title: Here’s What Really Happens to Your Clothes at the Dry Cleaner
articles.content:
You bring that stained silk blouse or rumpled blazer into the dry cleaner, drop it off with the attendant at the front desk, then come back a few days later (or more if, like me, you forget) to pick up your cleaned, pressed items, hanging neatly on a hanger and wrapped in plastic. It’s a ritual that has been going on for decades, but what happens once your clothing or linens leave your hands? Do they go on a whimsical ride through dry-cleaning land, where industrious elves work their magic? Sort of! Just replace elves with launderers and finishers, and you’re close.
To get the full picture, we spoke with Mike Astorino, who has more than 34 years of experience in the business and is the owner of Fabricare, a luxury dry cleaner in Fairfield County, Connecticut. Read on to find out exactly what happens to your clothes at the dry cleaner.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
It’s all about keeping certain delicate items in tip-top shape—and cleaning them without accidentally ruining them. For those items that need this VIP treatment, the pros use solvents in place of water and traditional laundry detergent to remove stains, sweat and grime from clothing.
That said, even when a care tag says something is “dry clean only,” that doesn’t necessarily mean it is. “In general, manufacturers are careless with their labels,” Astorino says. “Big, luxury brands will put very specific care instructions onto the garment and even test fabrics before going to market. However, for the thousands of other brands out there, ‘dry clean only’ is a way for them to deny responsibility if you wash an item and it shrinks or deteriorates.” (To wit, the $12 pair of purple track pants I recently bought that are labeled “dry clean only.” I could buy a new pair for the same cost as bringing them to the cleaner’s!) In some cases, you can even wash silk and wool—if you know what you’re doing.
But certain items are essential to dry-clean, such as anything with leather trim, a loose weave that runs the risk of snagging anywhere along the process, or an item with ornamentation like crystal buttons, Astorino says.
More than you probably think! Let’s take a little trip through a dry cleaner’s shop below.
“The cleaner looks for defects, such as loose buttons, torn hems and stains, and reports them to the customer,” says Astorino. “This protects us from things we didn’t do and allows us to repair the item to return it to the customer in a wearable condition.” Then each piece gets a unique tag, which is used to track it throughout the process to ensure it doesn’t get lost.”
At Fabricare, the tag is a small sticker with a bar code that attaches to the care tag, and customers don’t typically remove it. This gives the cleaners insight into some of the garment’s history, including how often it has been dry-cleaned, as well as the date of its last cleaning.
“To simplify removal, we classify stains into two categories: plant-based, like coffee, wine or tomato sauce, and animal-based, like sweat or blood,” Astorino says. To determine which is which, common sense comes into play. “Stains in the front of the garment are usually some type of food, whereas you’re more likely to find makeup around the neck, and mud or dirt on the bottom of dresses or pants,” he explains.
Then there are invisible stains, such as perspiration, perfume or light drinks like white wine. You might not notice them, but if they’re not treated promptly, they can ruin a garment. (These are typically removed through the regular dry-cleaning process.)
Beyond the stain, the cleaner needs to consider the fabric, the dye and the condition of the item before beginning to clean.
The machine dry cleaners use is similar to the one you use at home, save for a few key differences. It doesn’t use water, and it has far more settings for temperature and speed than your home washer. “The machines are computerized for different types of loads,” Astorino says. “Delicate silks will have a gentle cycle, while heavy coats and sweaters can handle more aggressive types of cleaning.” Solvent is added directly to the machine through a hose, the same way water is introduced into your machine at home.
The other big difference? Clothes are cleaned and dried in the same machine, he explains. Just like with dry-cleaner wash cycles, there are a number of different temperature and speed options for drying.
Oh, and a single machine costs around $60,000!
If a stain didn’t come out during the first cleaning, cleaners will try a different type of solvent. At Fabricare, this happens about 30% to 40% of the time, Astorino says. As a last resort, the cleaner may need to use water, which is an aggressive cleaner. “Cleaners are trained to start with the safest stain-removal technique and gradually get more aggressive,” he says.
There comes a point when continuing to clean a garment will actually damage it, and “that’s the first thing we train cleaners [to recognize],” Astorino says. “I learned from a high-end dry cleaner in New York when I first got in the business that ‘people come to us because we know what not to clean.’ Or put another way, we know when to stop.”
If a stain won’t budge in the traditional process, Astorino’s team communicates with the customer to let them know they can’t get their garment fully clean and potentially get approval to take more aggressive steps, as detailed above.
Once an item passes the cleaning department, it goes to finishing, which means “making the garment look like it did when you bought it,” Astorino says. “This is no easy task, especially with women’s garments. It requires knowing when to steam an item versus press it, or how to block a knit back to its original look. It’s really a craft.”
This is also the step when the item gets put on a hanger.
Here’s where automation generally comes into play. At Fabricare, the unique bar code is scanned, and the item is put on a conveyor belt, aka the device that looks like a sky liner for your clothes. The system knows it has, for example, one out of three of a customer’s items. So it spits out the item, bags it and waits to pair it with the other two items to group it and return it to the customer. Chances are, your local dry cleaner has a similar conveyor belt to bring items from the cleaning and finishing area to the front, even if the process isn’t fully automated.
At home, you use laundry detergent, which emulsifies stains so they can be rinsed away by water. In dry cleaning, fabric is cleaned with a solvent. The solvent works without water, to dissolve stains chemically. “Like water, the solvent helps lift soil from the fabric, which then gets flushed out through a rinse cycle,” Astorino says.
They’re safer now than they used to be. Decades ago, dry-cleaning solvents were perchloroethylene-based (a chlorine derivative), also called PERC. The system was different too—there were separate washers and dryers, so the solvent would drip from clothing onto the floor as the item was moved to the dryer, and that floor waste was considered toxic, Astorino says. While you may have read that PERC is harmful, and is a carcinogen, the chance of freshly dry-cleaned clothing negatively impacting your health is negligible. There is some evidence, however, that PERC was harmful to workers who came into direct contact with the chemical more regularly. Still, it’s always a good idea to remove the plastic from your clothes so they can air out.
Today’s dry cleaning is more environmentally friendly as a whole, in part because the EPA passed a ruling to phase out PERC-based cleaners fully by 2034. Today’s solvents are silicone- and hydrocarbon-based, neither of which is classified as a carcinogen, and silicone solvent is the same ingredient used in many everyday skin-care products. (Fabricare has been using these types of solvents since 2009).
Plus, more and more dry cleaners are moving toward a closed-loop system, which keeps the solvent inside the machine and reuses it, to cut down on chemical emissions and waste. This means “a very high amount of solvent is reclaimed and the rest is filtered out,” Astorino says.
Just like you wouldn’t wash your jeans after every wear, you don’t need to dry clean your sweater, blouse or suit jacket every single time. And thank goodness, because dry cleaning can be pricey! That said, you do need to clean clothing before putting it away for seasonal storage—remember, most stains are invisible and will set if you leave them. (Picture yellow armpit stains on a white blouse.)
The dry-cleaning process today is actually a pretty environmentally friendly way to get your clothes clean. It uses little to no water, and the newer solvents are gentler on you and the planet.
“Almost every type of wool or silk garment can be cleaned at home,” Astorino says. Options include wet washing (handwashing items in the sink or on your machine’s gentle cycle and drying flat) or investing in a DIY dry-cleaning kit. The latter typically includes a solvent you spray on your clothes prior to steaming them in your dryer.
In terms of what to try this with, use your common sense. You’ll want to be more careful with more delicate or meaningful items, like a “lucky” sweater or anything with leather trim or sequins. As for my bargain track pants? I’ve washed and dried them several times now, and they are just fine. (Phew!)

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE! Viola Davis Opens Up About the Health Battle That Changed Her Life and the Surprising Side Fans Rarely See
articles.content:
Viola Davis has never been one to shy away from a powerful role—or a difficult conversation. From her Oscar-winning performance in Fences to her riveting turn as Annalise Keating in How to Get Away with Murder, the EGOT-winning actress has spent decades bringing unforgettable characters to life. But behind all those larger-than-life characters is a woman whose own story of overcoming adversity is just as compelling.
In an exclusive interview with Reader’s Digest, Davis revealed the experiences that have shaped her, including how a battle with shingles changed the way she thinks about health and vulnerability. She also got personal about the role family plays in keeping her grounded and why there’s more to being strong than simply pushing through. Of course, we couldn’t talk to Davis without asking a few Hollywood questions too. Which character changed her life forever? And what’s one surprising thing fans would never guess about her from watching her on screen?
Read on for our candid conversation with Viola Davis, including the life lessons she’s picked up along the way and a few surprises you might not see coming.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more celebrity interviews, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
This interview took place on Oct. 8, 2026, and has been edited for length and clarity.
Reader’s Digest: You’ve played a lot of strong women—even people who are perceived as strong—but strength can mean something very different in real life. What does being a strong woman mean to you?
Viola Davis: Being a strong woman to me means being vulnerable, keeping my heart open to people and being honest about what I’m feeling at any given time. Being strong means knowing my worth, knowing when things bother me and when things don’t. “Hear me roar” doesn’t work for me anymore. I feel like it numbs too much of me, and I can’t numb anymore. I have a daughter, I have a life and I have friendships. I have love in my life. I have a husband. I want to have all my receptors open. Having shingles more than once was a wake-up call for me to redefine what strong is.
Reader’s Digest: You partnered with GSK Shingles to educate adults about their risk. What’s one thing you now understand about your health that you wish you’d understood before you experienced it?
Viola Davis: I had an unusual experience because I had shingles more than once. I had a blistering rash that wrapped around from my stomach to my back, then went away, then came back on my upper back. Nine out of 10 pain, easy. I couldn’t put my workout clothes on. I couldn’t put my regular clothes on. I had no energy whatsoever.
I felt like it was stopping me. It took me a minute to go to the doctor before they diagnosed me and told me that I was at risk and what I needed to do to prevent it. I was over 50 at the time. Once again, you’re in that area where you’re at an increased risk because your immune system is not the same. That’s why one out of three people get it in their lifetime. All of a sudden, I realize I’m not the woman king, even though I did The Woman King later in life.
I came to the realization that “You’re not 25 anymore, Viola,” so you have to take care of this beautiful aging body, and it’s OK when you know something is going on with it. It’s OK to go to the doctor, and it’s OK to bother them. You’re worth it. That was a hard one for me. I come from a long line of people who were just strong people. My mom worked in the field in Singleton Plantation from the time she was 4. So that was my wake-up call.
Reader’s Digest: Did having shingles change anything else about the way that you work—whether that’s now listening to your body, setting boundaries or allowing yourself some rest?
Viola Davis: I did not come from privilege, but I am privileged now. I started setting my hours, because you can do that once you reach a certain level in the profession. Being away from home for long, extended periods of time doesn’t work for me anymore. As soon as I finished a TV show, I would go home for two days and start a movie.
Imperfection is the key to connection. That includes admitting to yourself that you don’t feel so strong right now. Sometimes I think we feel alone with all of our thoughts and how we feel. We keep it locked up, and there’s something about vulnerability that lets it out. It seeks connection. I feel like that’s the best thing I’ve given to myself as I age. It’s the curiosity that life is more about the inside than the outside.
Reader’s Digest: I also imagine that these are pieces of advice that you want your daughter, Genesis, to understand as she gets older, too.
Viola Davis: I think the worst thing we can do is to betray ourselves, and I see women do that a lot. I can’t speak for men. They probably do too. We wear the mask that grins and lies. I tell Genesis all the time: “Do not betray yourself, no matter what. Disappoint everybody else in your life, but don’t disappoint yourself. If you need help, ask for it.” There is absolutely nothing wrong with that.
Reader’s Digest: While I’m sure that you’re teaching Genesis all these important life lessons, I know that she must have taught you some things herself. What is something that she’s introduced you to? It could be a phrase, a trend, a show, a song—anything that makes you feel like you’re truly a mom.
Viola Davis: The thing about young people today is that they are their own people, way more than my generation. I was taught to be the good girl—smile, say the good stuff and always be polite. I‘ve given my daughter permission not to do that. One day I said, “Genesis, you always have to have a language for how you feel. You have to be curious enough to name it.” She looked at me for the longest time, and she said, “I disagree with you. I think it’s OK when you don’t know how you feel.”
I think that it’s extremely liberating to be able to speak your truth, and speak your truth in in front of your mama. Mama and Daddy are the leadership positions in your life. She spoke her truth to me. So I learned something from that.
Reader’s Digest: You’ve spent years becoming other people, from Ma Rainey and Michelle Obama to Amanda Waller and more. Is there a character you played who you feel is surprisingly similar to who you are today, or maybe even the complete opposite?
Viola Davis: Annalise Keating [in How to Get Away with Murder]. She is everything that I’m not. She’s just unapologetic about her strength—unapologetic even about her vulnerabilities and flaws. I remember one line that Annalise Keating had when someone said, “No, you’re mistaken.” I say, “Oh, no, never. I’m never mistaken.”
There’s something about embodying all those character traits that I didn’t have that I always wished for. It sort of activated it in me, and it gave me permission to be all of those things. And I always say that instead of being a good girl, I wanted to be the girl that spoke her truth, even if it pissed people off, like Annalise Keating did. I wanted to stretch my boundaries and be unapologetic about all of my character traits—the good and the bad. She liberated Viola.
Reader’s Digest: What is something about you that would surprise someone who only knows you from the screen?
Viola Davis: Everything. First of all, I’m fun and funny. People have a blast at our parties. Number two, and once again, this is a contradiction, but I’m extremely introverted, probably to a fault. I’m extremely happy to just be a so-called “regular person.” I love throwing my slippers on and not wearing makeup—just getting in my car and doing my own shopping, cooking and everything on my own.
I am surprisingly simple. I don’t need a lot of things to make me happy. I don’t really need designer clothes. I hate shopping, except for perfume. I’m addicted to perfume.
Reader’s Digest: If you could preserve one completely ordinary moment from your life and experience it again 20 years from now, what moment would you choose?
Viola Davis: My husband will forgive me for this. I love him so much. But number one is kissing my daughter. Oh, my goodness! As a baby, kissing her on the lips. I would put her in that car seat every day. We’d go to the mall and the play area. Oh, man, I miss it.
*Editor’s note: Reader’s Digest does not endorse any specific products or services.
At Reader’s Digest, we’re committed to producing high-quality content by writers with expertise and experience in their field in consultation with relevant, qualified experts. We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. For this interview with Viola Davis, Reader’s Digest Associate Editor Mariah Thomas tapped her experiences as a celebrity interviewer, writer and editor. We verify all facts and data, back them with credible sourcing and revisit them over time to ensure they remain accurate and up to date. Read more about our team, our contributors and our editorial policies.

And I always say that instead of being a good girl, I wanted to be the girl that spoke her truth, even if it pissed people off, like Annalise Keating did. I wanted to stretch my boundaries and be unapologetic about all of my character traits—the good and the bad. She liberated Viola.

Reader’s Digest: What is something about you that would surprise someone who only knows you from the screen?

Viola Davis: Everything. First of all, I’m fun and funny. People have a blast at our parties. Number two, and once again, this is a contradiction, but I’m extremely introverted, probably to a fault. I’m extremely happy to just be a so-called “regular person.” I love throwing my slippers on and not wearing makeup—just getting in my car and doing my own shopping, cooking and everything on my own.

I am surprisingly simple. I don’t need a lot of things to make me happy. I don’t really need designer clothes. I hate shopping, except for perfume. I’m addicted to perfume.

Reader’s Digest: If you could preserve one completely ordinary moment from your life and experience it again 20 years from now, what moment would you choose?

Viola Davis: My husband will forgive me for this. I love him so much. But number one is kissing my daughter. Oh, my goodness! As a baby, kissing her on the lips. I would put her in that car seat every day. We’d go to the mall and the play area. Oh, man, I miss it.

articles.title: EXCLUSIVE! Author Fiona Davis Dishes on Bringing American Girl to an Adult Audience with Samantha: The Next Chapter
articles.content: If you were a child of the 1980s or later and played with dolls, chances are you owned—or wished for—an American Girl. There was Colonial-era Felicity, and Addy, who grew up during the Civil War, as well as bespectacled Molly, who dated back to World War II, and many more. Far from being just dolls, they had historical backstories, complete with books to go with them, and authentic clothing and accessories that were (and still are) as colorful as their lives. Believe it or not, the burgeoning brand—which was acquired by Mattel in 1998 and has since spawned an empire—is celebrating is 40th anniversary this year. And American Girl is marking the occasion with a new venture: Samantha: The Next Chapter, the first American Girl novel for adults. Yes, you read that right! But the delicious nostalgia is only the beginning. The story, set in New York City circa 1920, centers on the now-grown Samantha Parkington, an aspiring suffragist encouraging other young women to vote in their first presidential election. Her otherwise comfortable life takes an abrupt left turn when her inheritance is stolen and she sets out to save her family’s legacy. Adding to the fun? Fiona Davis, the bestselling author of The Stolen Queen, The Address and The Lions of Fifth Avenue, wrote the book and brought her expertise in New York–based historical fiction to the world of American Girl. We caught up with Davis just before the book’s launch to find out how she created grown-up Samantha’s story and why she thinks American Girl resonates with readers of all ages. Join the free Reader’s Digest Book Club for great reads, monthly discussions, author Q&As and a community of book lovers. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Reader’s Digest: What is your connection to American Girl? Were you a fan of the American Girl dolls or books growing up? Fiona Davis: I was in college when the first book came out, and I don’t have any kids of my own. Where I really connected with American Girl was through my nieces. My brother has three daughters, and all three loved American Girl, especially my niece, Erin. She loved Samantha best and the fact that she was very forward. Erin was shy, so having a doll whose character spoke her mind was very helpful for Erin, who was learning how to find her own voice. Reader’s Digest: How did you end up writing an American Girl book for adults? Fiona Davis: The company approached me and asked if I would write a book around Samantha. In a way, it was a gift not to know a lot about her because otherwise, I would have been paralyzed with fear. She is so loved, and the nostalgia around American Girl and Samatha is so strong. I think I was chosen because I know New York well. I write about historic New York, and the heroines in my stories are all very strong-willed. It was a good match that way. American Girl’s Janelle [Asselin] was my editor for the whole project and was brilliant. She reached out to me by email, which I reported to my agent and asked her if she thought it was a scam. She called them and said it was the real thing. So it all happened pretty quickly, and we were soon off to the races. Reader’s Digest: Was Samantha a departure from other characters you’ve written about? Fiona Davis: Samantha is a 25-year-old character, and I’ve had main characters who are around that same age as well. I had also worked on projects based in the 1920s. The fact that Samantha is very much into suffrage, even as a young girl, worked well because I had co-edited a group of short stories (Stories from Suffragette City) set around the suffrage parade in New York City in 1915; I have done a lot of research around that. On top of that, the town that Samantha grew up in is based on Mount Kisco, New York, which I know well. Reader’s Digest: Who decided Samantha would be the first adult American Girl to be featured in an adult novel? Fiona Davis: American Girl, the company, was very specific that Samantha would be the first. She was one of the first original dolls. Reader’s Digest: Did you read any of the original American Girl books while preparing? What was that experience like as an adult? Fiona Davis: I did a deep dive because the books are so important to her background. They introduce her family, her extended family, her community, her interests. It was really fun—and a gift not to have to make all that up. As an author, it was wonderful to have it right on the page and then see where it could go. Reading these books as an adult was enlightening; I wish I’d had them as a young girl. The sense of history comes through with such clarity. The characters are so wonderful. Reader’s Digest: Did any other American Girl stories really resonate with you? Fiona Davis: I also loved reading Addy’s story. I like the fact that the books don’t shy away from a difficult era in American history. But Samantha was my focus, for sure. Reader’s Digest: Did anything from this story speak to you on a more personal level? Fiona Davis: My parents are both English, so all our relatives lived in England. We lived in America since I was 3. Even though Samantha had lost her parents and was an orphan, she had such a loving extended family around her. I would have loved to have read these books as young child and experience the idea of having an extended family; I didn’t have that myself. Reader’s Digest: Was there a moment during the writing process when you felt especially aware of the full-circle nature of this project? Fiona Davis: I think it’s wonderful being able to reach beyond the original generation it was intended for. What’s interesting to me is whenever I have met an adult who knows the story, they get so excited. They always know where their American Girl doll is. It might be in their mother’s attic or their basement, and they always say, “Oh, yes, I’m a Samantha” or “I’m a Kirsten.” They identify so closely with the dolls and their characters. Reader’s Digest: Was it difficult adapting a character that so many people grew up with? Fiona Davis: The real challenge was staying true to her character as a child. Samantha is empathetic, tenacious and very intelligent. We needed to make sure that during all the stages—the research, writing and editing—that Samantha’s inner strength was still present. Meanwhile, she is an adult, having adult experiences. Readers need to know who the character is at her core and recognize that. Also, as a character, I had to have her undergo growth, so in the story, she’s maybe a little bit different than when she started. It’s the first time I’ve been handed a character and told to write a book about her. Reader’s Digest: This book will be such a hugely nostalgic story for a lot of readers. When crafting it, how did you balance nostalgia with telling a rich, complex story your way? Fiona Davis: I was lucky that I had a team of people behind me as I wrote. They not only included my editor but also a historian on staff at American Girl who supplied me with everything I needed to stay true to the time period. On top of that, they have a panel of consultants and experts and advisors on whatever subjects we were dealing with who could weigh in and make sure that the story was true to history. Their contributions are on every page of that book. I think that because it was this wonderful team effort, we carried that balance of nostalgia and growth throughout the plot. Reader’s Digest: Why do you think American Girl has such a lasting impact on so many of us? Fiona Davis: It’s because the American Girl team really cares about how the characters come across. They understand that they are affecting young girls, and there’s a huge responsibility there that they take very seriously. I think people who buy American Girl dolls understand that. That is why there is such brand loyalty. I think customers understand they are not being talked down to. The early stories are so fun to read, no matter what age you are. There’s a common thread throughout American Girl, no matter which character you identify with. With this book, the way I like to describe it is like going on a long road trip with an old friend. It’s somewhere new, but you have an old friend by your side the whole way. At Reader’s Digest, we’ve been sharing our favorite books for over 100 years. We’ve worked with bestselling authors including Susan Orlean, Janet Evanovich and Alex Haley, whose Pulitzer Prize–winning Roots grew out of a project funded by and originally published in the magazine. Through Fiction Favorites (formerly Select Editions and Condensed Books), Reader’s Digest has been publishing anthologies of abridged novels for decades. We’ve worked with some of the biggest names in fiction, including James Patterson, Ruth Ware, Kristin Hannah and more. The Reader’s Digest Book Club, helmed by Books Editor Tracey Neithercott, introduces readers to even more of today’s best fiction by upcoming, bestselling and award-winning authors. For this piece, Pamela Brill interviewed author Fiona Davis. We verify all facts and data, back them with credible sourcing and revisit them over time to ensure they remain accurate and up to date. articles.title: King Charles and Queen Camilla’s Nighttime Ritual Is Surprisingly Sweet
articles.content:
The relationship between Charles and Camilla, the king and queen of England, has been under a microscope for decades. Charles’s first wife, Princess Diana, who died in 1997, was pretty uniformly beloved, and Camilla was … well, let’s just say it took the public some time to warm up to her.
But despite how things went down all those years ago, it’s become clear that Charles and Camilla absolutely adore each other. They laugh at the same things, as she revealed last year on the couple’s 20th anniversary, and they enjoy spending time together even when they are like two “ships passing in the night,” as she told British Vogue a few years ago.
It makes one wonder why they didn’t just marry each other right off the bat, but that’s a whole other story. And everyone deserves happiness, right? Now, in a new documentary, the queen is opening up about a nighttime ritual that she shares with her husband, and it is so sweet and relatable, you might almost forget they’re royalty. Read on to learn what these two do to keep the love alive.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more royal news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Like a lot of couples, the king and queen read together every night. She divulged their charming routine in a new BBC documentary called The Book That Changed My Life. The documentary was produced in partnership with the Open University and Camilla’s charity, the Queen’s Reading Room, as part of the U.K.’s National Year of Reading.
“My husband and I actually read before dinner,” Camilla told the BBC. “We just like sitting quietly and reading.”
The queen went on to paint a picture of domesticity for the royal pair, describing how reading and their pre-dinner ritual are incredibly important to her. “It’s part of our heritage. If there’s no reading, personally, we might as well all give up,” Camilla said. “Because I don’t think we’d even be human anymore.”
He’s apparently not one to stay silent when reading, much to the queen’s dismay. “I, occasionally, when I’m deep in a book, hear him roaring with laughter about something,” Camilla said in the doc. “It’s very off-putting. I can’t get back into my book, or I’ll suddenly start weeping. But it’s a lovely, quiet time.”
She chalks up this quirk to the fact that Charles enjoys reading P.G. Wodehouse, the famed British humorist behind literary characters such as the quintessential English butler, Jeeves, and his employer, Bertie Wooster. Camilla, meanwhile, prefers thrillers and historical fiction, which aren’t exactly known for their laugh-a-minute hilarity.
Very. She points to her own early life spent reading and how it set her up for success when opportunities were limited. “I left school quite young, because in my day, women didn’t go to university,” Camilla said. “I think reading has been most of my education.”
The queen credits her father, Bruce Shand, with instilling a love of reading in her. “We must’ve been very, very young when my father started reading to us,” she said. “I think that’s where my love of reading came from.” She recalled reading Treasure Island and Peter Pan before graduating to A Tale of Two Cities, which she said coincided with her childhood fascination with the guillotine!
“I don’t think our childhood would have been the same if we didn’t have books,” she told the BBC.
The Queen’s Reading Room, which began as a book club during the COVID-19 pandemic and now reaches 12 million people in 183 countries, is an extension of her love of reading. But it’s about more than that: The Queen’s Reading Room also funds neuroscience research to study how reading and well-being are connected, and partners with other charities to provide books to people in the hospital or experiencing homelessness or domestic abuse.
Every year, Camilla highlights multiple must-read books on the Queen’s Reading Room website. She picks four books per season, or 16 books a year. Since 2021, she has recommended 64 books.
Despite her professed love of thrillers and historical fiction, her book list is quite diverse. Here are the highlights:

articles.title: Attention, Annoying Humans: You Might Be Interrupting Your Dog’s Sleep, According to a New Study
articles.content:
My sweet dog Willie Nelson is in his golden years—that long stretch of vaguely declining health and general slowing down that every pet parent braces for. Every night, he “jumps” (or, more often, is lifted) onto the bed and we snuggle in for a good night’s sleep filled with his snoring and snorting and kicking and rearranging … until I get up around 3 a.m. and move to the guest room.
Yes, sleeping with our pets can be problematic. But I would never kick him out: It’s not Willie’s fault I’m a light sleeper, and it took us forever to haul him up on the bed in the first place. And now, a new study confirms that co-sleeping has its downsides—not necessarily for you, but for your dog.
Ahead, I’ll take you through the results of this new research that totally upends what we think we know about humans, dogs and sleep. Read on to learn how your sleeping arrangements might be affecting everyone in your family, furry members included.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more pet news, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
Yes, we are, according to new research by scientists at the University of Toronto Mississauga. The study, which was published in Plos One, was on the small side, but it looked at 25 human participants and their 38 canine counterparts to find out how sleep patterns were affected by co-sleeping.
To do this, researchers outfitted dogs and owners with sleep monitors, and found that 61% of the subject “dyads” (aka the individual pairs of humans and dogs studied) moved together at some point in the night. But of that majority of interspecies co-sleepers who were in tandem, it was usually the human who moved first—not the dog.
Yep, in nearly half (45%) of the dyads that showed movement, it was the person who was doing the disturbing first. Could my dog, Willie, be off the hook for my banishment to the spare bedroom? I don’t quite believe it, but researchers have some pretty good numbers to back it up.
They measured both objective activity levels (using sleep monitors) and subjective variables, including the perception of sleep quality (which unfortunately our dogs can’t answer). They found that our belief that Fido is preventing us from sleeping, and not the other way around, might be a misperception, though the authors say more study is needed.
Researchers didn’t come to any conclusions about how these results could be affecting our animals. But as any of us who have been roused out of our REM cycle in the middle of the night—only to stare at the ceiling, attempt to count sheep or give up and read a book—can attest, lack of sleep is bad for you and, presumably, your dog too.
Sleep studies in dogs aren’t too common, but 2022 research published in Animals found that dogs who got less than eight to 10 hours of sleep were more likely to receive a higher “problem behavior score” by their owners. A 2025 study in Scientific Reports found that sleep can affect learning in dogs under certain situations, and an earlier one from 2017, published in the same journal, reported that dogs learn while sleeping, just like people do.
So given what we know about how important sleep is for humans, combined with this new data on dogs, it seems logical to conclude that sleep disruptions could be affecting their overall well-being, similar to how they affect ours. But sleep in dogs is still a relatively untapped field of study, so take everything with a grain of salt.
My anecdotal evidence aside, apparently not. Researchers in this study found that among the majority of participants whose sleep moves correlated with their dogs’ movements, the dogs moved first only 18% of the time. (Compare that with the 45% of the time we prompt movement in our pups.)
And when it came to objectively measured sleep patterns, like sleep duration and sleep efficiency in humans and overall nighttime activity in dogs, co-sleeping had no effect on either party. In the subjective measurements, humans reported poorer sleep only when they had more than one dog, even though the objective measurements didn’t back up their assumptions.
Interestingly, dogs that slept in the same room with their humans but not on the same bed were more likely to disrupt their owners’ sleep. Overall, researchers note the need for larger, more robust studies of dog-and-human sleep patterns. Willie and I will wait eagerly for this emerging research, but one thing I can tell you is that he’s not moving.
